content: As an alternative, other studies examining the relationships between folic acid intake, blood folate concentrations, and neural tube defect (NTD) risk were used to extrapolate the full relationship between intake, blood folate levels, and outcomes. A systematic search identified only one relevant case-control study, which included 84 NTD cases with blood folate concentrations. This study involved women attending their first antenatal clinic at one of three main maternity hospitals in Dublin, Ireland, between March 1986 and March 1990. Hospital records were used to select three controls per case from births without NTDs, for gestations of 23 weeks or more, in the same hospital and time period. Blood samples (median gestational age: 15 weeks) were analyzed for red blood cell (RBC) and plasma folate concentrations in 84 cases and 266 controls. RBC folate concentrations below 340 nmol/L were associated with an NTD risk of 66 per 10,000 live births. A Bayesian model confirmed the consistency of the dose-response relationship (increasing NTD risk with decreasing RBC folate concentrations) with findings from other populations, using data from China. Two populations from northern and southern China contributed data, including participants in a randomized trial evaluating the effect of folic acid supplementation on blood folate concentrations among women of reproductive age. The estimated NTD risk at various RBC folate concentrations aligned with NTD prevalence in the USA before and after mandatory folic acid fortification. The model concluded that a population RBC folate concentration of approximately 1,000 nmol/L is a threshold for preventing NTDs, consistent with previous findings. The overall quality of evidence for the association between RBC folate and NTD risk is low, according to the GRADE methodology. A systematic review of folate interventions assessed the response of serum/plasma and RBC folate concentrations to supplementation. For non-pregnant women of reproductive age, two reviews analyzed daily folate supplementation with folic acid or 5-MTHF and intermittent iron and folic acid supplementation. For pregnant women, one review assessed daily supplementation with folic acid or 5-MTHF. Data from Canada and Chile showed increases in median RBC folate concentrations after mandatory folic acid fortification. Similarly, data from NHANES in the USA demonstrated an increase in median RBC folate concentrations between preand post-fortification periods. It was estimated that a folate intake of 450 µg dietary folate equivalents (DFE) per day or higher could achieve the RBC folate concentration associated with the lowest NTD risk (~6 NTDs per 10,000 live births). While serum and plasma folate levels reflect recent intake, RBC folate indicates long-term folate stores. Serum folate responded to all interventions, while RBC folate responded mainly to supplementation and fortification. Understanding the response of serum/plasma and RBC folate to interventions will guide monitoring and evaluation efforts. Reviews on home fortification of foods with micronutrient powders and rice fortification with vitamins and minerals were identified but did not assess folate status. Chromatography-based techniques coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS/MS) are preferred for measuring folate vitamers due to their sensitivity and specificity. The choice of laboratory tests depends on the study type, specimen volume, and available resources. Precision in laboratory tests is critical for distinguishing between populations at risk of deficiency or with sufficient micronutrient status. At the population level, RBC folate concentrations above 400 ng/mL (906 nmol/L) in women of reproductive age are recommended to achieve the greatest reduction in NTDs. This threshold is useful for population-level assessments but cannot predict individual NTD risk. No serum folate threshold is recommended for NTD prevention at the population level. Microbiological assays are the most reliable method for obtaining comparable RBC folate results across countries. Quality control systems for RBC folate assessment using microbiological assays are essential for national nutritional surveillance. Differences in folate calibrators or microorganisms used in microbiological assays may necessitate adjustments to the optimal RBC folate threshold. The WHO guideline emphasizes the importance of reducing folate insufficiency at the population level to prevent NTDs. Dissemination of the guideline will occur through electronic media, social networks, and partnerships with international organizations. Monitoring and evaluation plans with appropriate indicators are recommended at all stages of implementation. Ethical considerations, including respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, and justice, should guide the adaptation and implementation of the guideline. Public health interventions should aim to achieve the highest attainable level of health and equity, particularly for vulnerable populations.
